l3.capacity.statement: The L3 is 32 MB: a 1 MB slice in each of the 32 compute shires, shared chip-wide and memory-side. The 5-bit home field means the master shire's cache is not an L3 home.
l3.capacity.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.13; driver_config.json `l3_kb` 32768; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.26 (five shire-ID bits for a 32-shire configuration)

l3.home.statement: A line's L3 home shire is PA[10:6]: consecutive 64-byte lines rotate over the 32 compute shires' L3 slices (default 'swizzle0'; the firmware leaves the swizzle register at reset).
l3.home.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.24 (§1.4.1.2) and p.26-27 (§1.4.3); external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:88-103; docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:373-377; memprobe: 1,500 lines, all but 2 within ±4 cycles of 110 + 12·hops(requester, PA[10:6]) (docs/et-soc1-notes.md:165)
l3.home.note: The IDs are virtual shire IDs; a spare-shire remap would move them (NOC_Remap_Shires).

l3.latency.statement: L3 hit: 110 + 12 cycles per mesh hop between the requesting shire and the line's home shire (fitted 110.5 + 11.99 on three cards); 159-169 cycles (265-282 ns) on average depending on the requesting shire.

l3.writearound.statement: Write-around stores coalesce in the L2's buffer and flush to the L3 once all four 16-byte qwords of a line are written (or on an explicit flush).

lat-dram.statement: DRAM load from a pointer chase: 287-297 cycles at 600 MHz (479-495 ns): 296.6-297.1 from shires 0 and 31, 287.2-288.8 from 7 and 24; about 490 ns, a fifth more than an A100's HBM (405 ns).
lat-dram.note: The value field is the slowest requesters (shires 0 and 31). At 800 MHz (aifoundry2 only) 352-368 cycles, 440-460 ns: the mesh and DDR parts do not scale with the minion clock.

lat-dram-chip.statement: Of a DRAM load's ~300 cycles only about 25-28 are the DRAM chip's own timing (activate tRCD 18 ns, 19.3 ns read latency, one or two 4.3 ns bursts); the rest is paths on the chip.
lat-dram-chip.source: docs/reports/2026-09-19-et-soc1-memory-anatomy.html section 4 ("Of the 91 cycles (152 ns), the DRAM chip itself accounts for about 25-28")
lat-dram-chip.note: From the controller's timing registers set against the fit; the memory shire (queue, PHY, clock crossings) is at most ~63-66 cycles.

lat-dram-refresh.statement: LPDDR4X refresh every 2,325 cycles (3.88 us) on every card; a load that meets it waits up to 208 extra cycles (347 ns).

lat-dram-rowconflict.statement: Two loads to the same bank but different rows, issued together: the second pays about +37 cycles (a2 36.9, a3 37.4, a1c1 36.5); bank = PA[12:10].

lat-dram-typical.statement: A typical DRAM load, timed one at a time: 299 cycles (500 ns), the median of 4,500 loads from shire 0 to random lines; 299 in each of 15 passes on three cards.

lat-l1.statement: L1 data cache hit: 5.25 cycles load-to-use (8.8 ns at 600 MHz); the same on three cards (per-pass ranges 5.247-5.259).
lat-l1.note: Only 512 B of L1 per hart: the firmware puts the L1 in scratchpad mode before every launch.

lat-l2.statement: L2 cache hit (and the shire's own scratchpad): 47 cycles (78 ns); hart 1 pays 3 more (39 read buffer, 50 L2).
lat-l2.note: The single-load ladder of Anatomy reads L2 at 49 cycles in every pass (a different probe and offset).

lat-l3-avg.statement: L3 hit from a pointer chase, averaged over all 32 slices: 159-169 cycles at 600 MHz (265-282 ns), by requesting shire: 168.8-168.9 (shire 0), 160.6-160.7 (7), 159.1-159.2 (24), 168.8-168.9 (31).
lat-l3-avg.note: The value field is the fastest requester (shire 24). Clock model: 72 cycles + 61 ns + 20 ns per hop.

lat-l3-hop.statement: L3 hit against distance to the line's home shire: 110.5 + 11.99 cycles per mesh hop (from shire 0), within 4 cycles for 99.4-100% of lines on each card.
lat-l3-hop.note: A local L3 hit is ~110 cycles: ~48 for the L1 and L2 lookup and miss, ~62 for the home slice (Anatomy, inferred). 31 of 32 L3 lines live in another shire.

lat-rb.statement: L2 read buffer (8 clean lines per bank x 4 banks = 2 KB per shire): 36 cycles (60 ns), 11 fewer than the L2 array.
lat-rb.note: Spec: 10 vs 21 shire cycles (CORE-ET Shire Cache Specification), per the memory-hierarchy page.

lat-scp-own.statement: The shire's own L2 scratchpad: 47 cycles (78 ns), the same SRAM, latency and bandwidth as the L2 cache.

lat-scp-remote.statement: Another shire's scratchpad: 99.84 + 12.00 cycles per mesh hop at 600 MHz (112-220 cycles, 186-366 ns over 1-10 hops); all 124 points within 1 cycle, a->b equals b->a within 0.032 cycles.
lat-scp-remote.note: Clock model (aifoundry2, 18 Sep): 66 minion cycles + 56 ns + 20 ns per hop.

mem.global-atomic.statement: A global atomic (amoaddg) is performed at the shire cache that homes the line. One contended line serialises at 10.00 cycles per atomic (about 60 M/s for the chip) and stops the host shire's own memory path; an uncontended remote global atomic round trip is 216 cycles.
mem.global-atomic.page: One hot line stops a shire

mesh-bit-mm-free.statement: A random bit per mm on free links, mesh rail at 0.485 V: 37 fJ (25 of it data-dependent); on board power 47 fJ. Dally's rule of thumb is ~100 fJ/b-mm.
mesh-bit-mm-free.note: Per card, mesh rail: a2 36.1, a3 35.8, a1c1 38.1 fJ; board 46.7, 44.4, 51.1 fJ (99% intervals in 05-claims). Scaled to 0.9 V the data cost is 85-105 fJ.

mesh-bit-mm-loaded.statement: On a busy mesh where flows share links the same random bit costs 53 fJ per mm on the mesh rail and 79 fJ on board power.

mesh-hop-lat.statement: Each mesh hop adds 12 cycles round trip at 600 MHz (20 ns): L3 11.99, remote scratchpad 12.00, TensorSend 12.01-12.02 cycles per hop on every card.
mesh-hop-lat.note: 20 ns at either clock (16 cycles at 800 MHz): a NoC-clock cost.

mesh-hop-ring.statement: TensorSend across the mesh: 9.2 pJ/B to leave the shire plus 1.75 pJ/B per mean hop (three cards pooled; a2 9.1 + 1.8, a3 8.0 + 1.7, a1c1 10.4 + 1.7); no card's per-hop cost differs from another's.
mesh-hop-ring.note: Straight line through five 1 KB rings (1.6-4.7 mean hops), six passes per card.

mesh.1kb-knee.statement: With 1 KB messages a round trip adds 12 cycles per hop up to 5 hops and 36 cycles (27-36) per hop beyond, as if the sender had a limited number of packets in flight.

mesh.clock.statement: The NoC runs at 400 MHz on these cards (every telemetry sample). The design's NoC clock is 500 MHz (from PLL2 in the I/O shire), and the firmware's DVFS table allows 300-500 MHz.
mesh.clock.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/horace-telemetry.jsonl (and horace2-, thermal-telemetry.jsonl: 3,681 samples, 20 Sep), field `mhz.noc`; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf, pdf p.12 (Table 2, clk__noc); external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/services/thermal_pwr_mgmt.c:134-135
mesh.clock.card: aifoundry2 (aifoundry3 set to 400 MHz by its boot service)
mesh.clock.cards_txt: aifoundry2 (aifoundry3 is set to 400 MHz by its boot service)

mesh.empty-cells.statement: Four cells of the 6 × 6 map hold no compute shire: (0,3), (0,4), (0,5) and (5,3). They hold the master, spare, PCIe and I/O shires and route traffic too; which cell is which is not established.
mesh.empty-cells.source: workloads/nocbench/analyze.py:60 (`EMPTY`); on-chip communication page §'Where the shires are'
mesh.empty-cells.note: The firmware's comment map (noc_reconfigure.h:76-90) puts PCIe/IO in one row and master/spare in another, but its shire placement matches the measured pairwise distances for only 254 of 1,024 shire pairs, so it cannot be used to label the cells.

mesh.grid.statement: The NoC is an 8 × 6 grid of mesh stops: 34 minion shires, 1 PCIe shire, 1 I/O shire and 8 memory shires; the four memory shires on each side leave the grid's corners empty, so there are 44 mesh stops.
mesh.grid.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.21 (§4 ET-SoC-1 Mesh Network on Chip)

mesh.logical-map.statement: Measured position of each compute shire on the 6 × 6 grid (marty1885's logical map, x across, y down): y=0: 0 24 9 25 2 11; y=1: 8 16 1 17 10 19; y=2: 3 4 13 14 18 27; y=3: _ 12 21 22 26 _; y=4: _ 20 29 30 15 23; y=5: _ 28 5 6 7 31.
mesh.logical-map.source: workloads/nocbench/analyze.py:52-60 (`MARTY`, `EMPTY`); docs/findings/05-claims.md:383, 412 (map recovered from latency alone in 12 of 12 search restarts on every card)
mesh.logical-map.note: Built by marty1885's etTopoScan from bandwidth on another card; confirmed by TensorSend latency on all three lab cards. Shire IDs are the firmware's logical IDs.

mesh.memshire-positions.statement: Fitted memory-shire positions on the logical map: memory shires 0-3 one step off the top edge at x = 1-4 (y = -1), 4-7 one step off the bottom edge at x = 1-4 (y = 6). Memory shire 2's position is a tie-break (x = 3 or 5 above the grid, or (6,0), fit equally).
mesh.memshire-positions.note: A fit of DRAM latencies with one constant (91 cycles) and 12 cycles per hop.

mesh.no-counters.statement: There are no NoC performance counters in the PRM, the firmware or core-et; mesh transit is inferred from latency differences.

mesh.orientation.statement: The logical map appears to be the die turned a quarter: in map orientation the memory shires sit above and below the grid, on the die (and in the firmware's naming, 0-3 west, 4-7 east) they are the two side columns.
mesh.orientation.source: docs/et-soc1-notes.md:102-105; anatomy page §1 'Trace one load'; settled 27 Sep by fw.map-match except the handedness (die.handedness)
mesh.orientation.note: Settled 27 Sep except the east-west handedness (facts fw.map-match, die.handedness).

mesh.port-width.statement: The shire cache's mesh master port is 512 bits wide (one 64-byte line per beat); a shire has four mesh lanes and a line goes to lane PA[7:6], so consecutive lines on one lane are 256 bytes apart; a flit carries at least one 64-byte line.
mesh.port-width.note: The inter-router link width and flit size of the NoC itself are not documented in the sources.

mesh.shortest-paths.statement: Round trips fit a + b × Manhattan distance on the map over all 496 shire pairs (worst residual 1.1-1.4 cycles), so routes are shortest paths through all 36 cells, the four non-compute cells included. The order was measured later, on 29 September: requests x first, replies y first (fact L104).
mesh.shortest-paths.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:381, 412; on-chip communication page §'What the numbers say'; anatomy page §1 ('the order in which the mesh routes a request was not measured'); the order: fact L104 (E56, docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr)

mesh.single-attach.statement: Each shire meets the mesh at a single point: minion 31 of each shire gives the same round trips as minion 0.
mesh.single-attach.source: on-chip communication page §'What the numbers say'

mesh.voltage.statement: NoC rail: set point 485 mV, 484-485 mV on die (per-shire 483-486 mV at idle).
mesh.voltage.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/horace-telemetry.jsonl (and horace2-, thermal-telemetry.jsonl: 3,681 samples, 20 Sep), fields `reg_mv.noc`, `die_mv.noc`; docs/findings/05-claims.md:41

mesh.xy-assumption.statement: The heat-per-mm analysis assumes dimension-ordered XY routing on the logical map (and checks YX); under it, links are shared by 0 / 22 / 32 / 55 / 72% of link-hops at 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 6 hops in the all-pairs traffic.
mesh.xy-assumption.source: workloads/enercat/analyze_wire.py:38, 149-176; docs/findings/05-claims.md:348 (WIRE `checks.link_sharing`); settled 29 Sep by fact L104 (E56)
mesh.xy-assumption.note: Settled 29 Sep: an analysis assumption, not a documented routing rule. E56 measured the order (fact L104): requests x first, replies y first, so a load's data travel y first (the YX case this analysis also checks) and a store's x first.

minion.combine-free.statement: Combining on receive (fp32/int32 add, max, min) adds 0 cycles to a round trip.

minion.etlink-width.statement: A minion's ET-Link request and response interfaces are 256 bits wide: the neighbourhood's request datapath is 256 bits, up-converted to 512 bits only at its output to the shire, and a 512-bit response reaches the minion as two 256-bit halves.
minion.etlink-width.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.15 (§4.3: 'The data size of the request datapath is 256 bits' ... 'a final up-conversion to 512 bits') and p.23 (§4.4.3: 'the Minion response interface is 256-bit wide')

minion.isa.statement: The ET-Minion is a dual-threaded (2 harts), in-order, single-issue RV64IMFC core with Zicsr and Zifencei and machine/supervisor/user modes; kernels run in U-mode.
minion.isa.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion Description.pdf, pdf p.5 (§2); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.7 (§2.1.1); external/et-man/ET Introduction.pdf, pdf p.7

minion.l1-firmware.statement: The firmware puts every minion's L1 in scratchpad mode before each launch, leaving each hart 512 B of data cache (2 sets × 4 ways × 64 B).

minion.l1-modes.statement: Three L1 modes (mcache_control D1Split, ScpEnable): shared (both harts, all sets); split (hart 0 sets 0-7, hart 1 sets 14-15); scratchpad (hart 0 sets 12-13, hart 1 sets 14-15, sets 0-11 become a 3 KB = 48-line tensor scratchpad).
minion.l1-modes.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.245-246 (§8.3.1, Table 8.4)
minion.l1-modes.note: The Minion Overview slide draws split mode as 2 KB per hart; the PRM table is followed here.

minion.l1-port.statement: The data cache can feed one register-file entry of all 8 VPU lanes (32 bytes) in a single cycle.

minion.l1d.statement: Each minion has a private 4 KB L1 data cache: 16 sets × 4 ways × 64 B lines, not coherent with any other cache, writing back whole 64-byte lines.
minion.l1d.source: external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.1 (slide 2); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.9 (§2.1.1.5)

minion.miss-handlers.statement: Two miss handlers per minion, so at most 2 outstanding cacheable line misses; tensor loads keep up to 4 L2 transfers in flight; there is no prefetcher.

minion.msg-cost.statement: A one-way message stream costs a fixed 40 / 86 / 135 / 224 cycles per message plus 2.3 / 4.0 / 3.0 / 4.6 cycles per 32 B register on the fast network / shire crossbar / mesh at 1 hop / mesh at 10 hops.
minion.msg-cost.source: on-chip communication page §'Message size and bandwidth'

minion.no-divide.statement: No hardware divide or square root in U-mode: fdiv.ps and fsqrt.ps trap, as do sine, reciprocal square root, 64-bit float conversion and reading the cycle CSR; 161 of the instructions tried execute in U-mode, 13 trap.

minion.one-ready-bit.statement: The hardware keeps one peer-to-peer ready bit per minion, not one per partner: a minion receiving from two TensorSend partners at once hangs its hart permanently (the card then needs a reset).
minion.one-ready-bit.note: sys_emu tracks every partner separately and does not reproduce the hang.

minion.sleep-unused.statement: The minion's sleep and isolation ports (nsleepin, iso_enable, nsleepout) are marked 'not used'; in the open Erbium RTL they are tied off and no firmware drives them. Idle cores are clock-gated, not power-gated.
minion.sleep-unused.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion Description.pdf, pdf p.7 (interfaces table); docs/findings/05-claims.md:177-179
minion.sleep-unused.page: The DVFS loop and its leakage

minion.tenb-tenc.statement: TenB is virtually 16 registers × 64 B (1 KiB), physically much smaller, and only streams loaded data to a consumer; TenC is 16 × 64 B (1 KiB) of int32 accumulators visible only to integer tensor multiplies.
minion.tenb-tenc.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.264

minion.tensor-cache-path.statement: Tensor loads skip the L1 but are cached in the L2 and L3; tensor stores skip the L1 and the L2.
minion.tensor-cache-path.source: docs/energy-manual/04-bytes-memory.md:21, 38; the L2: docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-memp2/val-aifoundry3/memp2.json, val-aifoundry2/memp2.json and dev-aifoundry1-c1/memp2.json .cards.<card>.items.R36.medians (tl1, tl2, ref_l2, ref_l3, probe_tl)
minion.tensor-cache-path.note: Settled 29 Sep for the L2: E57 (R36) TensorLoaded the same fresh 1 KB twice, and the second load took 199 cycles, the L2 reference's 199 (the L3 reference 744, the first load 1,344.5), and a scalar load after it 42, an L2 hit, on aifoundry3, aifoundry2 and aifoundry1-c1: a TensorLoad that misses allocates its lines in the L2. Not measured: whether the L3 keeps them and whether tensor stores skip the L2 (the Shire Cache Specification says they do).

minion.tensor-csrs.statement: Tensor instructions are CSR writes that run asynchronously: tensor_fma 0x801, tensor_load 0x83F, tensor_load_l2 (TensorLoadL2Scp) 0x85F, tensor_quant 0x806, tensor_store 0x87F, tensor_reduce 0x800 (TensorSend/Recv/Broadcast/Reduce), tensor_wait 0x830.
minion.tensor-csrs.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.272-274 (§9.3)

minion.tensor-hart0.statement: Only hart 0 of a minion may issue tensor instructions; hart 1 may only issue TensorLoadL2Scp, TensorWait and tensor_coop accesses.
minion.tensor-hart0.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.264

minion.tensor-shape.statement: A TensorFMA computes C[M][N] += A[M][K] · B[K][N] with M, N ≤ 16 and K ≤ 64 / (bytes per element): A from the L1 scratchpad, B streamed through TenB, C accumulated in hart 0's vector registers (int8 in TenC). One fp32 op is 4,096 multiply-adds.
minion.tensor-shape.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.264 (§9); docs/et-soc1-notes.md:292-294

minion.tensorfma-546.statement: With A and B both in the L1 scratchpad a 16×16×16 fp32 TensorFMA takes 546 cycles (fp16 546, int8 318), identical for every data pattern.

minion.tensorload.statement: TensorLoad reads up to 16 rows of 64 contiguous bytes (64 B aligned, row stride in x31) from memory into consecutive L1-scratchpad lines, bypassing the L1 data cache; a mask can skip rows.
minion.tensorload.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.273 and p.275 (§9.3.1, TensorLoad)

minion.tensorsend.statement: TensorSend moves COUNT consecutive vector registers (32 B each, up to 127, wrapping past f31: about 4 KB) from the issuing hart into hart 0 of a target minion anywhere on the chip; the receiver's TensorRecv can add, max or min the data into its registers at no extra cost.
minion.tensorsend.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.272 and p.311-314; on-chip communication page (headline); docs/findings/05-claims.md:380-381

minion.vec-peak.statement: The tensor instructions run on the vector unit's own lanes: each of the 8 lanes holds the FMA (TxFMA) and the two int8 multiply-add (IMA/TIMA) units, and state machines in the VPU sequence the multi-cycle tensor operations on them. An 8-lane fmadd.ps does 16 FLOP per cycle, the same fp32 peak as TensorFMA.
minion.vec-peak.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.8 (§2.1.1.2: TxFMA, a pair of IMA units and 'Finite state machines that generate long sequences of vector operations to implement multi-cycle tensor operations'); external/core-et/docs/Minion VPU Specification.pdf, pdf p.11 (§2: TXFMA and two TIMA units per lane); scripts/ridge-points.py:46, 51 (fp32 TensorFMA and vec32 fmadd.ps, per_cycle 16 each)

minion.vector-rate.statement: A simple vector-FMA loop reaches only about 1.5 lane-FMAs per cycle per minion; the best published vector-unit matmul is 2.94 TFLOP/s at 650 MHz (FOSDEM 2026), against the tensor unit's 9.5.

minion.vpu.statement: The vector unit has 8 identical 32-bit lanes in lockstep; the 32 FP registers f0-f31 are 256 bits wide (8 × fp32) per hart. Each lane has one FMA unit (one fp32 or two fp16 multiply-adds per cycle), two integer multiply-add units (four int8 multiply-accumulates each), one integer unit and one transcendental unit (exp2, log2, reciprocal).
minion.vpu.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.8 (§2.1.1.2); external/core-et/docs/Minion VPU Specification.pdf, pdf p.11 (§2) and p.33 (§2.2.5.2: 16 TIMA lanes); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.2 (slide 3)

minion.vpu-pipeline.statement: The VPU pipeline has eight stages.

minion.vpu-regs.statement: Each lane's register file holds 64 × 32-bit entries (32 per thread), so each hart has 32 vector registers of 32 bytes; 8 mask registers of 8 bits.
minion.vpu-regs.unit: vector registers per hart (32 B each)
minion.vpu-regs.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion VPU Specification.pdf, pdf p.11; external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.8-9

mm-board-w.statement: Board power during the fp32 L2 matmul that runs at 9.51 TFLOP/s, idle before the run plus the watts over idle: aifoundry2 33.3 + 25.7 = 59.0 W (die 80 °C), aifoundry3 26.0 + 24.4 = 50.4 W (62 °C), aifoundry1-c1 41.83 + 27.25 = 69.1 W (75-76 °C): 50.4-69.1 W across the three cards (die 62-80 °C). 9.51 TFLOP/s over these is the 161, 189 and 138 GFLOP/s per W of the same run (138-189).
mm-board-w.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:418 (E37, MMB-c: docs/reports/data/2026-09-25-claims-v3/results/mmb.json .items[item=MMB-c].per_card.<card>["fp32-tensor-L2"].board_w, .idle_before_w, .mean, .die_c_mean) and :419 (MMB-d, GFLOP/s per W)
mm-board-w.note: The sum is this page's; 05-claims.md gives the watts over idle and the idle before each run. Idle power moves with the card and its temperature (26.0-41.8 W here).

mm-peak.statement: Tensor peak per minion-cycle: 16 fp32 / 32 fp16 / 128 int8 ops; 9.83 TFLOP/s, 19.7 TFLOP/s and 78.6 TOP/s on 1,024 minions at 600 MHz.

mm-perw.statement: Board GFLOP/s per W, L2 matmul fp32 / fp16 / int8: aifoundry2 161 / 316 / 1,172; aifoundry3 189 / 370 / 1,377; aifoundry1-c1 138 / 270 / 958 (each card at its own die temperature).
mm-perw.note: Against the A100 spec sheet (peak / TDP) at full fp32 precision the card is 3.3x (a2), 3.9x (a3), 2.8x (a1c1) more energy-efficient on the benchmark's +-1/+-2 operands; the A100's int8 tensor cores lead by 1.13-1.63x.

mm-rate.statement: Tensor matmul, tiles in L2, all 1,024 minions at 600 MHz: 9.51 TFLOP/s fp32, 19.02 fp16, 71.77 TOP/s int8, the same on each card (91-97% of the 9.83 / 19.66 / 78.6 peak); 529 cycles per fp32/fp16 op, 280.35 per int8 op.
mm-rate.note: Every result bit-exact against a host reference.

mm.dram.statement: The same benchmark with 64 private tiles per minion, so that every load comes from DRAM: 15,042-15,663 cycles per op and 0.309-0.312 TFLOP/s on the three cards, about 30 times slower than with the tiles in the L2.

mm.reload.statement: The matmul benchmark loads a new A (16 lines from the shire's L2 into one of two L1-scratchpad buffers) and streams B through TenB before every TensorFMA, issuing the next op's loads while the current FMA runs, and it takes 529.001 cycles per op on all three cards: no more than the TensorFMA alone with B through TenB (529.05-529.09 cycles), so the next A's load of about 160 cycles is hidden behind the FMA.
mm.reload.note: A version that waits for each load before its FMA was never run; 160 + 529 cycles for it would be a derived figure, not a measured one.

mm.w-3cards.statement: The same matmul on the three cards (ABL-T8, watts above zeros at the board): ones 8.52 [7.70, 9.34], 8.09 [7.33, 8.86], 9.00 [7.33, 10.66] W and random data 25.33 [24.49, 26.17], 23.91 [23.51, 24.30], 26.66 [24.85, 28.48] W (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; 99% intervals): ones cost 8.1-9.0 W more than zeros and random data 23.9-26.7 W more. The registered test passed on aifoundry2 and aifoundry3; aifoundry1-c1 is reported against aifoundry2's registered values.

mm.w-data.statement: The Horace runs of the fp32 matmul, 9.18 TFLOP/s on every data set (timed from the host over the whole run, its launches included), launched at 80.6-81.0 °C on aifoundry2: 38.29 W on zeros, 46.73 W on ones and 63.40 W on random data, the board's power at the launch temperature: its reading in seconds 1-3 of the run (38.29, 47.56 and 65.80 W) less the leakage that the run's own heating had added by then, at the fitted leakage slope. Idle before each run: 36.3 W.
mm.w-data.unit: W at the launch temperature (random data)
mm.w-data.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-21-horace-aifoundry2/horace3.json: patterns.<zeros|ones|randn>.p80, .p_early, .p_before, .tflops, .start_temp; tools/ettelem/analyze_horace_strict.py:105-116 (tflops over t_start of the first launch to t_end of the last), :141 and :275 (p80 = p_early - leak x (t_early - launch temperature))
mm.w-data.note: Leakage-corrected, not a raw board reading: the raw mean board power over the random-data runs was 66.73 W.

ms-fit-3cards.statement: Left as fitted on aifoundry2 on 19 September (constant 91 and the memory-shire places, not refitted), the DRAM latency model is within ±3 cycles for 93-97% of loads on all three cards: aifoundry2 97.0%, aifoundry3 92.9%, aifoundry1-c1 94.4% (5 passes each).

ms2-forced.statement: Memory shire 2's fit ties (3, -1), (5, -1) and (6, 0), but (5, -1) is a corner of the 8 × 6 grid, and the corners are empty, while (6, 0) lies outside the grid: within the fit's assumptions (3, -1) is the only place left.
ms2-forced.source: L42 (docs/reports/2026-09-19-et-soc1-memory-anatomy.html:778-780); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.21 (§4: 'the corners of the grid are not occupied')
ms2-forced.note: The logical map is 6 rows (x = 0-5) by 8 columns (y = -1 to 6, the memory shires at y = -1 and 6).

neigh.composition.statement: A neighbourhood is 8 minions sharing a 32 KB L1 instruction cache (128 sets × 4 ways × 64 B), two L0 micro-I-caches (each shared by 4 minions, 16 fully associative 512-bit entries) and a 12-counter PMU.
neigh.composition.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.11-13 (§2.1.2); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.3 (slide 4)

neigh.coop-tload.statement: Cooperative TensorLoad: identical tensor-load requests from minions (across the neighbourhoods of a shire) are synchronised and coalesced into one memory request; cooperative TensorStore combines pairs or quads of minions writing one line.
neigh.coop-tload.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.273-274 (§9.3.1.1, §9.3.5.1); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.3

neigh.fln-edges.statement: The fast local messaging network links minions within a neighbourhood only along the reduction tree: 0-1, 0-2, 0-4, 2-3, 4-5, 4-6, 6-7.
neigh.fln-edges.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.26 (§4.7 Fast Local Messaging Network)

neigh.fln-latency-spec.statement: Messages on the fast local network see a 3-cycle response-path latency and take priority over regular fill responses; every other message leaves the neighbourhood and returns through the shire crossbar.

neigh.pmu.statement: The neighbourhood PMU implements 12 counters: 6 shared by the even harts (hart 0 of each minion) and 6 by the odd harts; mcycle and minstret read 0.
neigh.pmu.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.10 and p.12 (§1.3, §1.3.2)

neigh.ptw.statement: Two page-table walkers per neighbourhood are drawn in the architecture but not implemented in the first silicon revision.
neigh.ptw.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.11 (footnote 1)

op-600.statement: Base operating point: minion clock 600 MHz at 0.517 V on die (median while a kernel runs, aifoundry2). A warm card is held here by the governor; every table in the reports is at this point.
op-600.note: Minion rail voltage at 600 MHz by card: 518 mV (aifoundry2), 522-523 mV (aifoundry3), 499 mV (aifoundry1-c1) (manual.json catalogue.rail_mv; 01-at-rest.md "The three cards").

pcie.conc.statement: Two host-to-device commands in flight on one stream move 6.09 / 6.09 / 6.03 GB/s (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1), half the 12.39 / 12.48 / 12.28 GB/s of one command at a time (two streams with both of each stream's commands in flight, four in all: 5.96 / 6.00 / 5.96 GB/s in total; with one command in flight in each of two streams nothing is lost, 1.012 of one at a time on aifoundry3, 1.014 on aifoundry2 and 1.019 on aifoundry1-c1, E55); both directions at once, one command each at a time, move 16.97 / 16.89 / 16.92 GB/s together (2 × 64 MB per stream, DMA only).
pcie.conc.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: conc.<card>.dma.h2d.agg_gbs.mean (no barrier: both commands of the stream in flight), ."h2d/ser" (a barrier on every copy), ."2xh2d", ."h2d+d2h/ser"; E55: docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-pcie2/pcie2.json .cards.aifoundry3.stats.s2 and .h64 (and .cards.aifoundry2, the third card), .theories["T35-S"]; dev-aifoundry1-c1.md P35-6
pcie.conc.note: E55 (29 September) found which commands collide: two in flight in one stream move 0.488 of one at 2 x 64 MB on aifoundry3, one in each of two streams 1.012 (T35-S; on aifoundry2 0.496 and 1.014); a shared read engine, the IOMMU, a fixed cost per overlap, a slow onset and a loss per element were refuted on all three cards.

pcie.d2h.statement: Device to host, DMA only, 256 MB per copy: 10.54 [10.43, 10.64] GB/s on aifoundry2, 10.41 [10.30, 10.52] GB/s on aifoundry3, 10.41 [10.38, 10.45] GB/s on aifoundry1-c1: 10.41-10.54 GB/s, 66-67% of the link figure, slower than host to device. The fastest device-to-host size is 16 MB on aifoundry2 (11.75 GB/s), 16 MB on aifoundry3 (10.99 GB/s), 16 MB on aifoundry1-c1 (10.69 GB/s).
pcie.d2h.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: bw.<card>.d2h.dma[bytes=268435456].gbs; the size of the largest bw.<card>.d2h.dma[].gbs.mean

pcie.h2d.statement: Host to device, DMA only (the runtime's host-side copy replaced by a no-op, the analogue of pinned memory), 256 MB per copy: 12.47 [12.39, 12.55] GB/s on aifoundry2, 12.60 [12.55, 12.65] GB/s on aifoundry3, 12.46 [12.41, 12.50] GB/s on aifoundry1-c1 (mean of 5 runs [99% interval]): 12.46-12.60 GB/s, 79-80% of the link's 15.75 GB/s.

pcie.launch.statement: An empty kernel on all 32 compute shires, launched and waited for: 566 / 556 / 565 µs (556-566 µs) from launch to completion (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1); 100 launches queued back to back: 103.6 / 103.7 / 104.1 µs each (103.6-104.1 µs) on 32 shires and 91.2 / 92.2 / 92.4 on one shire. The card's own cost is the queued figure: a lone launch waited for adds 463 / 452 / 461 µs (452-463 µs, each run's difference), most of the runtime's 500 µs idle poll (fact pcie.poll), and a one-shire lone launch takes the same 566 / 556 / 565 µs.
pcie.launch.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: launch.<card>.single_us."32".mean, launch.<card>.b2b_us."32".mean, .b2b_us."1".mean, .single_us."1".mean; predictions[id=P9b].per_card.<card>.value.mean (launch to completion minus back-to-back, per run)

pcie.link.statement: Host link: PCIe Gen4 x8 on an x16 card edge; the datasheet gives up to 128 Gbps each way (25.78 Gbit/s per lane PHY). 15.75 GB/s per direction is the Gen4 x8 figure; the transfers were timed on three cards on 27 September (facts pcie.negotiated, pcie.h2d).
pcie.link.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.4 (§1); external/et-man/ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf, pdf p.3; docs/findings/05-claims.md:489; docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json (27 Sep)

pcie.negotiated.statement: The link trained at 16.0 GT/s x8 on all three cards in every run (sysfs current_link_speed and current_link_width): PCIe Gen4 x8, 15.75 GB/s per direction after 128b/130b coding.

pcie.nhalf.statement: A DMA-only host-to-device copy reaches half its 256 MB rate at 2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 MB per copy (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; n½, from the mean over five runs of log2 of the size): smaller copies are dominated by the per-command time.

pcie.poll.statement: The runtime's response thread polls the device's completion queue, sleeping 50 µs between polls while commands are in flight and 500 µs when none are.
pcie.poll.note: aifoundry3 runs a patched libetrt.so and aifoundry1 a fork build, so their constants may differ (PREREG.md).

pcie.small.statement: A 4 KB copy issued after a random 0-1 ms gap takes 377 / 379 / 411 µs on average (377-411 µs; aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; the mean over the four copy variants), while 200 queued 4 KB copies take 38 / 13 / 30 µs each (host to device, staged) and a wait on an idle stream 2.6 / 0.4 / 2.3 µs. The time of a lone small copy is the runtime's response polling, not the link.

pcie.staged.statement: The path a program takes, the runtime's staged copy (a host memcpy into a CMA bounce buffer, then the DMA), 256 MB: host to device 7.15 / 5.20 / 7.79 GB/s (5.20-7.79), device to host 6.53 / 4.78 / 6.97 GB/s (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1). The hosts' own memcpy runs at 17.4 / 9.2 / 21.4 GB/s, and each staged rate is 98-100% of 1/(1/DMA + 1/memcpy): the runtime copies and then transfers, one after the other, so a slow host memcpy (aifoundry3's) cuts the staged rate on the same link to 0.67-0.73 of the other hosts' (host to device).

pcie.write-l3.statement: A host-to-card copy goes through each line's L3 home, which allocates the line: after a staged 4 MB copy, 99.5% of the lines read at L3 latency on aifoundry3 (99.6% on aifoundry2, 99.9% on aifoundry1-c1), whether the L3 held the buffer before or not, and every value read was the last one written. A kernel's first touch of a freshly copied buffer hits the L3, not DRAM (tested for a 4 MB buffer).
pcie.write-l3.source: tools/claims-v3/pcie2/PREREG.md (frozen 29 Sep 00:04 PDT, sha256 f632d6b3...); docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-pcie2/pcie2.json .cards.aifoundry3.stats.fw and .fc (h2d_warm, h2d_cold: the share of lines whose first touch is L3-like), .stats.bad (wrong values), .theories["T34-A"]; .cards.aifoundry2 the same (the third card); dev-aifoundry1-c1.md P34-7, P34-8 (card 1, development)
pcie.write-l3.note: E55's T34-A (29 September). The rivals, an L3 that updates only lines it already holds (T34-B) and writes that go to the memory shires with the L3's copy invalidated (T34-C) or left stale (T34-D), were refuted on all three cards. When the L3 writes the lines back to DRAM was not timed; flow 6 draws that leg dashed.

power.idle.statement: Idle card after 20.6 h with no workload: 31.79 W at 73 °C, of which minion rail 11.05 W, SRAM 2.00 W, mesh 3.64 W and 15.10 W on no sensor.
power.idle.page: The DVFS loop and its leakage

relay-13x.statement: Handing a slab to the next shire through its scratchpad costs 12.9x, 13.0x and 13.1x less energy per byte than the DRAM round trip (aifoundry2, aifoundry3, aifoundry1-c1): about a thirteenth, the same on every card at 99%.
relay-13x.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-25-claims-v3/results/rl.json: items[RL-d, part=relay DRAM / next shire].per_card.<card>.ratio_geo_mean; docs/findings/05-claims.md:451
relay-13x.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

relay-bw.statement: Relay bandwidth (8 stages, 1,024 minions): 47.7 GB/s through DRAM, 592.5 GB/s to the next shire (12.4x), 1487 GB/s in the own scratchpad (aifoundry2 pass means; the other cards within 1.5%).
relay-bw.note: Speed-ups 12.25-12.42x (next shire) and 30.8-31.2x (own scratchpad) over DRAM; the advantage needs the live data to outgrow the 32 MB L3 (below it 1.4-1.5x).
relay-bw.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM
relay-bw.cards_txt: aifoundry2 pass means (the other cards within 1.5%)

relay-energy.statement: Relay energy per byte (write + read): through DRAM 116.2 pJ/B [104.5-135.3], to the next shire's scratchpad 8.9 [7.6-10.2], in the own scratchpad 4.3 [3.8-5.1].
relay-energy.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

relay-watts.statement: The three relay media draw within a watt of each other over idle (4.34 / 4.42 / 5.30 W for DRAM / next shire / own): the relay's energy saving is time, not power.
relay-watts.note: The 22 Sep session's power block (onchip.json power).
relay-watts.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

relay.speedup.statement: A multi-stage pipeline that hands each stage's output to the next shire's scratchpad runs about 12.4× faster than one that goes through DRAM (31× keeping it in the own scratchpad), at 116 / 8.9 / 4.3 pJ per byte moved (DRAM / next shire / own).
relay.speedup.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

ridge.levels.statement: Ridge points at 600 MHz (fp32 FLOP per byte fetched): own shire L2 or scratchpad 4, L3 or another shire's scratchpad 10, DRAM 130, PCIe 624 at the link figure of 15.75 GB/s; at the measured host-to-device DMA rate (12.46-12.60 GB/s, fact pcie.h2d) the PCIe ridge is 780-789.
ridge.levels.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:486-489; the measured-DMA ridge computed in build_facts.py: 1,024 minions x 16 FLOP x 600 MHz (facts chip-minions, minion.vec-peak, op-600) over docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json bw.<card>.h2d.dma[bytes=268435456].gbs.mean

sc.l3-miss.statement: An L3 read from another shire enters the home shire's cache through its L3 slave port and moves down the pipeline as L3_Read and L3_Fill: a miss goes out the to_sys mesh port to memory, the data comes back as the L3 fill, and the home answers the requester. The order memory shire, L3 home, requester is the specification's; which way each leg turns on the mesh is not documented.
sc.l3-miss.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.55 (§3.2.2 'L3 REQ_Read': 'They are received from the L3_slave and move down the pipeline as L3_Read and L3_Fill. Misses and victims are directed to the to_sys mesh port.', Figure 14)

scp.format0.statement: Scratchpad address, format 0 (bit 30 = 0): 0x80000000 + (shire << 23) + offset, shire ID in bits 29:23, offset in bits 22:0; shire ID 0x7F means the requester's own shire. A request whose shire field is not the local shire goes out over the to_l3 mesh interface to the target shire.
scp.format0.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.486 (§15.3); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.10, p.24 (§1.4.1.3); external/et-platform/et-common-libs/include/system/layout.h:71-76; docs/et-soc1-notes.md:88

scp.format1.statement: Scratchpad address, format 1 (bit 30 = 1, minions only): the shire ID sits in bits 29:28 and 10:6, so consecutive 64-byte lines land in different shires' scratchpads.
scp.format1.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.486 (§15.3)

scp.offset0.statement: Offset 0 of a shire's scratchpad faults; a global atomic through the local-scratchpad ID 0x7F is a bus error.
scp.offset0.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

scp.size.statement: Each shire's scratchpad is 2.5 MB (0x280000 in the firmware); 80 MB over the 32 compute shires.
scp.size.page: Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

shire.bank-queues.statement: Per bank: a 64-entry request queue (up to 21 entries reserved for L3-slave requests), an 8-entry read buffer and a 32-entry write-around coalescing buffer; L3-slave requests take priority over local L2 requests.
shire.bank-queues.source: docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:458-465; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.9 (coalescing buffer, 32 entries per bank) and pdf p.36 (arbitration)
shire.bank-queues.page: One hot line stops a shire

shire.cache-geometry.statement: The shire cache is 4 MB: 4 banks × 1 MB, each bank 4 sub-banks; L2 and L3 are 4-way set-associative, 64-byte lines, write-back and write-allocate, with SECDED ECC on tags, data and state.
shire.cache-geometry.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.8-9 (§1.1: 'The POR for the first SoC is 4M/Shire, 4 banks/Shire, 4 sub-banks/bank'); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.13 (§2.1.3.1)

shire.composition.statement: A minion shire is 4 neighbourhoods = 32 minions = 64 harts, a four-bank 4 MB shared L2/L3/scratchpad cache, a mesh stop, a crossbar between them, and an uncacheable (UC) block with fast local barriers, fast credit counters, inter-processor interrupts and global atomics.
shire.composition.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.5 (§2.1); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.4 (slide 5)

shire.crossbar.statement: A full request crossbar joins the 4 neighbourhoods and the RBOX to the 4 banks and the UC block; each bank has five 512-bit L2 input ET-Link buses, one 512-bit L3 input bus from the NoC, and two outputs toward the NoC: 'To L3' and 'To System' (main memory).

shire.l2-bw-spec.statement: Spec L2 bandwidth: four banks × 64 B = 256 B per shire-cycle, i.e. 8 B per minion-cycle, 4.9 TB/s on 1,024 minions at 600 MHz.

shire.neigh-link.statement: The 8 minions of a neighbourhood share one 512-bit ET-Link bus to the shire cache and UC block; responses reach a minion over a 256-bit bus (a 512-bit line takes two cycles).
shire.neigh-link.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf, pdf p.11 (§3.2); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.22-23

shire.other-modes.statement: Other defined partitions (chip totals, scratchpad / L2 / L3): M1 0/64/64 MB, M2 0/124/4, M3 0/128/0, M4 128/0/0, M5 64/64/0; software can change mode only after evicting and stopping the minions.

shire.partition-m0.statement: Mode M0, the reset mode and the one these cards run: per shire 2.5 MB scratchpad, 512 KB L2, 1 MB L3 slice; over 32 shires 80 MB scratchpad, 16 MB L2, 32 MB L3.
shire.partition-m0.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.21-22 (Tables 6-7, 'The chip will come out of reset in mode M0'); external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:106 ('default cache config mode = M0'); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.4

shire.partition-measured.statement: The driver reports L2 16,384 KB, L3 32,768 KB and scratchpad 81,920 KB in total on every card, i.e. mode M0; line size 64 B, 4 L2 banks.

shire.sc-latency-spec.statement: Idle shire-cache latencies in shire clocks, crossbars included: read-buffer hit 10, L2 read hit 21, L2 miss 34 + NoC and L3/memory, L3 read hit 30 (at the slave), L3 miss 42 + NoC and memory.
shire.sc-latency-spec.note: Measured load-to-use is 36 (read buffer) and 47 (L2) minion cycles; the difference is the minion pipeline, L1 miss and neighbourhood path.

sram-idle.statement: SRAM rail at idle (leakage of the L2/L3/scratchpad arrays): 1.60 W at 67 C, 2.63 W at 82 C on aifoundry2; slope 0.066 W/C on aifoundry3.

sync-allreduce1024.statement: Hardware allreduce of 32 B over all 1,024 minions: 1,393 cycles (2.3 us), 1,392.6-1,393.4 on the three cards; an A100 grid.sync() alone is 1.1-1.2 us.

sync-allreduce32.statement: Hardware allreduce (TensorReduce + TensorBroadcast) of 32 B over a shire's 32 minions: 444 cycles (0.74 us), 444.06-444.31 on all three cards.

sync-chip-barrier.statement: Chip-wide barrier built from FLB, global atomics and credits: 4,976-4,991 cycles with one minion per shire, 4,998-5,013 with all 1,024 (about 8.3 us); the allreduce tree does it in 2.3 us.
sync-chip-barrier.note: Energy: about 10 uJ of waiting (1,024 stalled minions at 1.2 mW for the barrier's length; derived, energy manual section 6).

sync-shire-barrier.statement: Shire barrier (fast local barrier + credits, 32 minions, all 32 shires at once): 233 cycles (388 ns); 232.5-232.7 on the three cards.

sync.fcc.statement: Fast credit counters: two per hart (four per minion); any hart in any shire adds credits by writing a 64-bit mask to a shire's CREDINC0-3 ESRs; reading an empty counter blocks until a credit arrives.
sync.fcc.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.328 (§11)

sync.flag-memory.statement: A flag handed through global atomics in memory costs 610-1,150 ns round trip (median 873), whatever the distance: it depends on which shire's L3 slice holds the flag's line.
sync.flag-memory.source: on-chip communication page §'Latency grows with distance, except through memory'

sync.flb.statement: Fast local barrier: 32 barrier counters per shire, 8 bits wide (enough for all 64 harts), joined atomically with one CSR write (0x820) from user mode.
sync.flb.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.327 (§10)

sync.tree-levels.statement: Each allreduce tree level adds about one round trip: 68-71 cycles on the fast network (levels 0-2), 117 through the crossbar (levels 3-4) and 164-234 over the mesh (levels 5-9).

tfma.tenb.statement: A 16×16×16 fp32 TensorFMA with B streamed through TenB instead of held in the L1 scratchpad: 529.05-529.09 cycles on all three cards (A in the L1 scratchpad).

tl.all.statement: All 1,024 minions tensor-loading at once: 256.0 cycles per 16-line load from the L2, and 7,994-8,037 cycles from DRAM (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1: 8,037 / 7,994 / 8,021), where the memory shires set the pace.

tl.one.statement: One minion's TensorLoad of 16 lines (1 KB) into its L1 scratchpad: 160.4 cycles from the L2 and 160.1 from the own scratchpad, on all three cards; 4 lines from the L2 take 41.9 cycles. From DRAM, 16 lines take 748-751 cycles on passes 2 and 3 and 1,132-1,133 on the first pass.

ts-credit.statement: Credit-counter (FCC) round trip: 140.2 + 14.43 cycles per hop (234 ns + 24 ns/hop); blocking credit inside a shire 119.5-119.9 cycles (200 ns).
ts-credit.note: The registered prediction (148 + 12.2) failed: credits rise 24 ns per hop, not 20.

ts-e-pair.statement: Messaging energy, 1 KB TensorSend: 0.69 pJ/B between the two minions of a pair, 2.16 around a neighbourhood, 2.22 around a shire, 12.5-18.3 across the mesh (busy cores included).
ts-e-pair.note: 128 B messages cost more: 3.66 pJ/B around a shire, 20.2 to the next shire ID.

ts-rt-fln.statement: TensorSend round trip, 32 B register to register inside a shire: 68 cycles (113 ns) on the 7 fast-network tree edges of each neighbourhood, 114-115 cycles (190 ns) for every other pair.
ts-rt-fln.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:380; docs/reports/2026-09-18-et-soc1-on-chip-communication.html "Inside a shire, only the tree edges are fast"
ts-rt-fln.note: Same pairs and same cycles in every pass on all three cards.

ts-rt-mesh.statement: TensorSend round trip between shires, 32 B: 150 + 12.02 cycles per mesh hop (250 ns + 20 ns/hop), worst residual 1.1-1.4 cycles over all 496 shire pairs; 1 KB messages add 12 cycles per hop to 5 hops and 36 beyond.
ts-rt-mesh.note: The shire map (marty1885's) is recovered from latency alone in 12 of 12 search restarts.

volt.minion.statement: Minion rail: set point 520 mV, 516-518 mV on die under load at 600 MHz; per-shire 517-521 mV at idle. Firmware limits 400-620 mV (boot default 500).

volt.other.statement: Other rails, set point / on die: DDR 800 / 762-768 mV, Maxion 600 / 583-586 mV, I/O shire - / 751-754 mV, PCIe shire - / 749-753 mV (PCIe logic set 775 mV), VDDQ 1,100 mV, VDDQLP 640 mV.
volt.other.note: The firmware's boot default for the Maxion rail is 850 mV (thermal_pwr_mgmt.h:97); these cards run it at 600 mV.

volt.sram.statement: SRAM rail (shire-cache arrays): set point 705 mV, 703-707 mV on die.
volt.sram.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/horace-telemetry.jsonl (and horace2-, thermal-telemetry.jsonl: 3,681 samples, 20 Sep), fields `reg_mv.sram`, `die_mv.sram`; docs/findings/05-claims.md:41

lanes4.t: 4 to_l3 master and 4 L3 slave lanes

layout.mesh_orientation: logical map, x across (index within a row) and y down (row index), as drawn on the on-chip communication, memory anatomy and spatial temperature pages; 'grey' = no compute shire

asks.part: die view: every die position (the logical map turned onto the die)
asks.what_is_inferred: How the measured logical map sits on the die: logical x as die rows, y as die columns, memory shires 0-3 on the west, and the east-west sense (distances cannot tell a rotation from a mirror).
asks.what_settles_it: Mostly settled by firmware source already in hand: the firmware's 'default Shire Virtual ID Map, based on the NOC spec' (noc_reconfigure.h:76-82), renamed by the boot firmware's NOC_Remap_Shires (main.c:284; 'No displacement' table noc_reconfigure.h:398-405, used when no shire is fused off), equals the measured map cell for cell with no rotation or mirror: 496 of 496 pair distances and 32 of 32 cells (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json). So the diagram's die view L34 is exactly the NoC-spec drawing: memory shires 0-3 on the left (west), PCIe then I/O at the right (east) end of the top row, as PRM Fig. 1-3 and datasheet Fig. 2-6 also draw it. Fact L37 ('does NOT match') compared the map before the renaming and is superseded. Still open: whether the silicon has this handedness or the published die plot's (I/O then PCIe, the mirror); a floorplan with labelled mesh stops, a die plot with its orientation stated, or the package ball map settles it.
asks.ask_detail: top-level floorplan or an oriented, scaled die plot (AI Foundry); second source: the ET-SoC-1 Data Book / a final datasheet with the ball map

asks.part: the four grey cells (master, spare, PCIe, I/O)
asks.what_is_inferred: Which grey cell is the master shire (32), the spare (33), the PCIe shire and the I/O shire.
asks.what_settles_it: Settled by the same firmware map (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json grey_cells): logical (0,3) = shire 32, the master (top row, die column 4); (5,3) = shire 33, the spare (bottom row); (0,4) = the bridge map's 'pcie0'; (0,5) = 'io0' (noc_reconfigure.h:84-90). This is L32's alternative reading (PCIe west of I/O, as PRM Fig. 1-3). To confirm on the cards: time SYSCALL_PMC_SC_SAMPLE on shire 32 from each compute shire (a + b x hops picks the top or bottom cell). E56 did so on 29 September (docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr, hub rung 31): on aifoundry1 card 1 shire 32 placed at (0,3), the firmware's cell (rms 1.1 cycles; the next cell, (0,4), 33.1); on aifoundry3 and on aifoundry2, the third card, the calls' cost missed the frozen fit rule for a constant plus a term per hop (rms 4.7 and 4.47 cycles, at most 4 allowed), so the cell was not decided there, and the rule reports a place only when every card run agrees. PCIe/I/O order rests on the two firmware comments and the PRM; the NoC spec would confirm it.
asks.ask_detail: exp-mesh-stops; the NOC spec that the firmware maps cite

asks.part: memory shire placement (memory shire 2 a tie)
asks.what_is_inferred: The memory shires' places come from a DRAM-latency fit on one card; memory shire 2's fit ties three places and is forced by elimination.
asks.what_settles_it: The firmware map puts mc0-mc3 on the west at rows 1-4 and mc4-mc7 on the east at rows 1-4 (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json memshires): the fit's places for the 7 memory shires it places on its own, provided the firmware's mcN is the memory shire selected by PA[8:6] = N. With those 7 in place memory shire 2 has one cell left in both, so the map confirms the frame, not memory shire 2 on its own. What settles it on the cards: time SYSCALL_PMC_MS_SAMPLE (ms 0-7) from each of the 32 compute shires; each call's cycles are a constant plus a per-hop term to that memory shire, with no L3-home leg (the confound behind the tie). E56 did so on 29 September (docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr, hub rung 31): on aifoundry1 card 1 memory shires 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 placed where the firmware map puts them, memory shire 2 at (3,-1), and 3 and 6 were not decided; on aifoundry3 and aifoundry2 nothing was decided (the calls' cost missed the frozen fit rule, as for the grey cells).

asks.part: the mesh's routing order (every route the eleven flows draw)
asks.what_is_inferred: Measured on 29 September (E56, fact L104): a request goes x first and its reply y first, back along the request's links; the diagram draws every route so (before, it drew every leg x first). Still inferred: which of a flow's packets travel as requests (TensorSend, TensorReduce and TensorBroadcast are drawn x first, like a store's data; E56 timed only tensor loads and stores), and the router-to-router flit width (L105 note).
asks.what_settles_it: Settled for loads and stores by experiment: E56 ran sets of 1 KB tensor-load and tensor-store streams that share one directed link under one order and none under the other, frozen before the validation (tools/claims-v3/nocr/PREREG.md; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr). On aifoundry1 card 1, aifoundry3 and aifoundry2 the loads slowed only where their replies would share a link under y first, the stores only where their data would share one under x first, and a shared link carried about 92 GB/s. What is left: the same sets with TensorSend streams would place the tensor messages; the NoC configuration's generated reference manual (noc/reference_manual/noc_reference_manual.htlm, named at core-et rtl/inc/debug_defines.vh:831-832), the Main NoC documentation linked from CORE-ET Minion Shire Description §3.3 (pdf p.11, link missing) and the 'NOC spec' (noc_reconfigure.h:76, 84) would give the rule for every packet and the flit width. Interface: the routers' VC-status registers (noc_esr.h RIVCS/ROVCS), SP-only.

asks.part: the way back of a DRAM load (Flow 1, Load -> DRAM)
asks.what_is_inferred: The reply's path: the diagram draws it from the memory shire through the L3 home to the requester, each leg y first.
asks.what_settles_it: The leg order is documented in a manual already in the repo: CORE-ET Shire Cache Specification §3.2.2 'L3 REQ_Read' (pdf p.55): L3 reads that miss go out the to_sys mesh port, the data returns to the L3 as L3_Fill, then the reply goes to the requester, so memory shire -> L3 home -> requester is spec. Each leg's route: a reply goes y first (E56, 29 September, fact L104), so the drawing takes each leg back along its request's links. What is left: E56's streams ran between compute shires' scratchpads, so that a memory shire's and an L3 home's replies follow the same rule is inferred.
asks.ask_detail: cite the Shire Cache Specification; exp-route-order (E56) for the route of each leg

asks.what_is_inferred: Was: 15.75 GB/s per direction, the Gen4 x8 link figure, with host transfers never timed.
asks.what_settles_it: Settled on 27 September: timed on three cards with workloads/pciebench, five runs per card against predictions stated before the runs (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie; the page Over the PCIe link). Not a team ask.

asks.what_is_inferred: Measured on 29 September (E55, fact pcie.write-l3): the host's writes go through their lines' L3 homes, which allocate the lines. After a staged 4 MB copy 99.5% of the lines read at L3 latency on aifoundry3 (99.6% on aifoundry2, 99.9% on aifoundry1 card 1), whether the L3 held the buffer before or not, and no value read was stale. Still inferred, and drawn dashed: the L3's later write-back of those lines to the memory shires and DRAM.
asks.what_settles_it: Settled by experiment: copy a buffer from the host, then time each line's first load in a kernel launched without the L3 flush; L3-hit latency means through the L3 homes (tools/claims-v3/pcie2/PREREG.md, frozen before the validation; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-pcie2). What is left: why the bridge sends the writes there. The PCIe shire's to-sys bridge has DRAM address-map entries for every shire's L3 slave (SHn_L3D) and for each memory shire (MC0..MC7_MEM) (etsoc-hal hwinc/noc_esr.h, BRIDGE_PS0_TOSYS ... MAP_MEM_DRAM), so the programmed ADBASE/ADMASK decide: read them (SP-only) or the NoC documents.

asks.part: the DRAM address map below the memory shire
asks.what_is_inferred: PA[9] channel, PA[12:10] bank, PA[34:18] row, decoded from firmware ADDRMAP values and a tool comment, and measured on 29 September (E57, fact L50): another row in the same bank conflicts, and a row that also differs in any of PA[6-12] reads as a row hit, on aifoundry1 card 1 and aifoundry3 (R33a), and in 14 of 15 conditions on aifoundry2, where two lines that differ only in PA[17], a column bit in the map, read as a row conflict; PA[6-9] set the refresh phase, so each controller refreshes on its own, on aifoundry3 and aifoundry2 (R33b; not established on card 1). Still open: whether two accesses on one controller serialise (R33c, insufficient on all three cards), and why PA[17] conflicts on aifoundry2.
asks.what_settles_it: Settled for the banks and rows by experiment: single DRAM loads with every line evicted first, timed against the rows and banks the map predicts (tools/claims-v3/memp2/prereg/PREREG.md, frozen before the validation; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-memp2). What is left: the controller's serialisation (R33c's method did not resolve 6 cycles), the refresh domain on card 1 and PA[17] on aifoundry2; a service-processor readback of each controller's ADDRMAP registers would settle the whole map.

asks.part: the DRAM chip's share of a load (memory shire panel)
asks.what_is_inferred: About 25-28 of a DRAM load's cycles are the DRAM's own timing; the rest on-chip (timing registers set against the fit).
asks.what_settles_it: A memory-shire description with its pipeline latencies (NoC bridge, uMCTL2 controller, PHY, clock crossings) or a readback of the programmed DRAMTMG registers; or, as an experiment, DRAM latency at a second DRAM clock (needs a build: mem_controller.c:643 fixes 933 MHz; 800 and 1066 modes exist).

asks.part: the tensor unit's cache path (tensor sequencer, L1 scratchpad)
asks.what_is_inferred: Tensor loads skip the L1 but are cached in L2 and L3; tensor stores skip the L1 and L2 (energy manual; PRM confirms only the L1 bypass). The L2 part is measured (E57, 29 September): a second TensorLoad of the same 1 KB took 199 cycles, the L2 reference's 199, on aifoundry3, aifoundry2 and aifoundry1 card 1. Not measured: whether the L3 keeps the lines, and the stores' bypass.
asks.what_settles_it: Mostly documents already in the repo: CORE-ET Shire Cache Specification §3.5 'REQ_WriteAround' (pdf p.62): TensorStores issue writeArounds that bypass the L2 (coalesced in its buffer, written to the L3 or a remote scratchpad); Minion DCache Description: TensorLoad requests go out the L2 miss interface (pdf p.32) and fill the L1 scratchpad straight from the L2 interface (pdf p.41). Whether the L2 allocates tensor-load lines: settled by the re-load timing test (tools/claims-v3/memp2/prereg/PREREG.md, R36; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-memp2). What is left: the L3's copy, by the same test with the L2 evicted between the loads, or shire-cache counters.
asks.ask: document (in repo) + experiment (done for the L2)

asks.part: the UC block, the I/O shire and the shire's voltage regions (one-line descriptions)
asks.what_is_inferred: Not inferred, but thinly sourced: the UC block and the I/O shire's Maxions are drawn from one line of text, and the sources disagree on the Maxions' cache (4 MB in the datasheet and the PRM, 1 MB in the Shire Cache Specification).
asks.what_settles_it: The design documents the open drop cites but leaves out: Power Spec, UC Specification, Shire Bus Master Specification, PLL/DLL Initialization, MAS: Minion Shire Debug, Debug High-Level Specification, Debug Memory Map, Minion CSRs, DFT Specification, Maxion Shire MAS, Maxion Tile MAS.

asks.part: the host link's open questions (PCIe shire, Host, Flow 6)
asks.what_is_inferred: Not inferred but unexplained, from the PCIe page: why two host-to-card DMA commands of one stream at once move half as much as one, and why card-to-host DMA dips at 32-64 MB per copy. E55 (29 September) found where the loss is: two commands in flight in one stream move 0.488 of one at 2 x 64 MB on aifoundry3, one command in each of two streams 1.012 (T35-S; 0.496 and 1.014 on aifoundry2), and a shared read engine, the IOMMU, a fixed cost per overlap, a slow onset and a loss per element were refuted on all three cards tested. aifoundry3's host copies memory at about half the others' rate because it runs one memory channel (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/hosts.txt).
asks.what_settles_it: What serves one stream's two commands in turn: the runtime's source for a stream's DMA queue, or the master minion's DMA worker in the firmware; the PCIe DMA engine's documentation, or the settings the firmware programs (channel arbitration, read-request size, element splitting), for the card-to-host dip; the lab admin's reads on the hosts (lspci -vvv for the payload and read-request sizes).
